Today, we release d1-3B and d1-omni-600M, two open-weight models in our d1 decision model family .

d1-3B scores 48.57 on the Decision Index v0.2.1 (public split), ahead of every model under 10B and on par with Decider 35B-A3B, a decision model 12x its size. It runs the full NVIDIA stack, from DGX in the data center to Jetson at the edge: d1-3B answers a question in 8 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, 16 ms on a Jetson AGX Thor, and 26 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin. Even the Jetson Orin Nano runs it in 50 ms, fast enough for real-time decisions on the smallest edge hardware.

d1-omni-600M is our first experimental checkpoint, handling both text and image, as well as text and audio. It scores 15.95 on the same index.

d1-3B and d1-omni-600M models are available today on Hugging Face. Check out our docs on how to run them locally.

## Architecture and Training

Unlike our generative Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), our d1 decision models don’t produce tokens. Instead, they produce an answer in a single forward pass.

d1-3B and d1-omni-600M are trained from two very different backbones:

- d1-3B is trained from LFM2.5-VL-3B , our latest VLM, which is decoder-only. It accepts text and images as inputs.

- d1-omni-600M is trained from LFM2.5-Encoder-350M , a bidirectional encoder. It adds vision and audio encoders to handle all three modalities. It accepts either text and image, or text and audio as inputs.

d1-3B. We averaged the weights of LFM2.5-2.6B and the text backbone of LFM2.5-VL-3B to create a better base model. We then fine-tuned checkpoints with different random seeds and data mixtures before merging them again. Training on long inputs, shuffling answer options, and fixing shortcuts in the data made a bigger difference than more advanced techniques.

d1-omni-600M. We first fine-tuned LFM2.5-Encoder-350M on decision tasks, then added audio and vision in stages. For audio, we trained a FastConformer encoder with an adapter to connect it to the backbone, then fine-tuned the audio encoder with a frozen text backbone. For vision, we took the encoder from LFM2.5-VL-450M and trained an adapter plus LoRA updates to the backbone. Those updates were active only when the input included images, and the vision encoder stayed frozen. We then fine-tuned the full model, merged the LoRA updates, and averaged the weights with the previous checkpoint to regularize the final model.

## Fast Inference Everywhere

d1-3B and d1-omni-600M run the full NVIDIA stack — from DGX in the data center, to RTX workstations, to Jetson at the edge — with day-one support for llama.cpp.

Since decision models don’t generate output tokens, we measure end-to-end latency, from input to output. We report inference numbers for d1-3B. d1-omni-600M is an early research release and is under active development.

## Open d1 in Action

These results make our small open d1 decision models a strong fit anywhere you need fast, structured decisions, including multimodal inputs. d1-3B delivers the highest decision quality at its size, while d1-omni-600M fits where footprint matters.

To show what real-time decisions look like in practice, we built ten demos that run our open d1-3 B in a loop over live camera input, from gesture-controlled games to live content moderation, each reading answers from one pass per frame. You can try them out in our Hugging Face space without any setup.

In collaboration with NVIDIA, we also demonstrate d1-3B navigating an environment in Isaac Sim, with the model served on a Jetson in a hardware-in-the-loop setup.

- Fast from day one — Native support for llama.cpp across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and NVIDIA with NVFP4

- A family — Two sizes let you trade accuracy for footprint as your deployment demands.

Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B .

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

## What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

## Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

## Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

- llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference

- MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon

- vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput

- SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework

- ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on Pipette , the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.

We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.

## Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.

The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.

Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face .

For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.

- Fast from day one — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware

Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3 , our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face , our Playground , and the Liquid AI API . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

## New architecture for more expressivity

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention could run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. Its design came from our automated hardware-in-the-loop architecture search . For LFM3, we used this search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts.

We also expanded the hardware in the loop, from CPUs in one phone and one laptop for LFM2 to 14 device and backend combinations for LFM3: phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15), a Raspberry Pi 5, laptops (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen AI), and Arm and x86 cloud CPUs, plus GPUs and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

Gated short convolutions still make up over half the layers. To add capability without slowing down long contexts, we tried swapping some of them for other sequence blocks, and sliding-window attention (SWA) gave the best quality–speed tradeoff. We kept the other changes described below only where they improved quality without a meaningful speed cost. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster.

Tri-hybrid layer mix. LFM3 combines three operators: gated short convolutions, sliding-window attention (SWA), and global attention. Of its 24 layers, 13 are convolutions, 5 are SWA with a 256-token window, and 6 are global attention. The convolutions also use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.

Head-wise gated attention. A sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization and improve training stability .

Partial RoPE. Global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head and leave the low-frequency half unrotated, so those dimensions match on content regardless of distance . SWA layers keep full RoPE.

Sandwich norm. Each block normalizes both its input and its output, which helps keep activations well-scaled.

LFM3 uses the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B , built to tokenize non-Latin scripts more efficiently.

Training. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens. Compared with LFM2, the mix adds more scientific papers, repository-level code, a wider range of knowledge sources, and considerably more math. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated, higher-quality data, with a larger share of agentic traces and diverse tool calls to prepare the model for agentic post-training. This stage also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

## A multimodal family for every need

The first LFM3 release includes six models, all branched from the same LFM3-1.7B-Base backbone and all around 2B parameters. Four of them cover different input modalities (text, vision, audio, and omni), and the last two are decision models specialized from the vision and omni models. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you can pick the one that fits your use case, customize it, and run it on-device.

For a deeper dive into the performance and inference results behind these models, refer to the respective model cards.

> As AI increasingly moves from the cloud to the client, developers need models that can be deployed efficiently across the broad spectrum of AI PCs. Liquid AI's LFM3 family combines strong multimodal capabilities with a compact footprint that is well suited for on-device AI experiences. AMD has worked closely with Liquid AI across multiple generations of models, and we're excited to see LFM3 expand what's possible for specialized AI applications running locally on systems with AMD Ryzen™ AI processors.

> Across industries, we’re seeing edge AI evolve from running dedicated detection and perception models to supporting multiple concurrent AI workloads, including vision-language models, natural-language interfaces and multimodal reasoning. The challenge is delivering these capabilities within the compute, memory, and power constraints of edge devices. LFM3 brings text, vision, and audio together in a unified architecture designed for efficient deployment, with open weights that developers can fine-tune for specific applications. Developers can already run Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-VL models on Ambarella silicon through the Cooper Model Garden, and we have begun enabling LFM3 on the same platform.

> The next generation of AI will be more multimodal, personalized, and private while being distributed across devices and the cloud. Liquid AI’s LFM3 family is an exciting step in that direction, and we’re pleased to work together to bring fast, efficient, and innovative AI experiences to devices powered by Snapdragon® processors.

### Text

LFM3-1.7B is a text model for local agents and specialized applications with a 256K-token context window.

It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It can triage your inbox, manage your calendar, research topics on the web, send you morning briefings on WhatsApp, and use tool search to find the right tool among thousands of options. Since tokens are free, dozens of agents can run continuously in the background. You can adapt it to your domains, harnesses, and tools with a short fine-tuning run on a single GPU.

On agentic tasks, LFM3-1.7B competes with models several times its size. It leads on instruction following and function calling on BFCL and ToolSandbox, and beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps (WebArena-Verified, AutomationBench). Larger models still win on agentic coding and knowledge, where size matters most, but search helps close the knowledge gap, nearly doubling its score on Humanity's Last Exam.

To achieve these results, the model went through four stages of post-training:

- Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): 1.75T tokens across various tasks, including chat, reasoning, tool calling, and agentic traces.

- Mixed reinforcement learning: many domains trained at once, from math and code to SQL and structured outputs. A length penalty in the reward keeps answers concise.

- Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD): six specialist RL teachers (code, math, tool use, long context, agentic work, and enterprise workflows) are distilled back into a single model.

- Agentic RL: tasks from web browsing to office work are run inside real agent harnesses, preparing the model for deployment.

On-device, we measure metrics with llama.cpp at Q4_0 and a 32K-token context. LFM3-1.7B is the fastest model on all three devices, decoding 1.8 to 2.8 times faster than the next one, and it uses the least memory. Long contexts stay cheap: a full 128K-token context needs 1.6 GB of KV cache, against 4.3 GB for Qwen3.5-4B and 5.6 GB for MiniCPM5-2B.

On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-1.7B can produce 3.6 billion tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests, more than any other model in this comparison.

To show what this throughput makes possible, we ran more than 300,000 LFM3-1.7B agents in parallel to investigate the Enron email archive.

LFM3-1.7B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like online fraud detection when run on Liquid RIPL . P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.

> We tested LFM3-1.7B against Qwen3.5-2B on 65 everyday agent tasks in real macOS environments. The smaller model won: 64% task success versus 48%, 58% fewer tokens per task, and it got stuck in under 1% of attempts versus 15%. Small models are ready for real agent work on the Mac, and LFM3 is the proof. LFM3 is the first sub-2B model we’ve tested that is ready for real agent work on a Mac — it beat a larger model on task success while using 58% fewer tokens and almost never getting stuck.

### Vision

LFM3-VL-2B can watch, reason, and understand the physical world:

- Video understanding: for the first time, an LFM vision model takes video as input. Ask questions about a recorded lecture, a walkthrough filmed on your phone, or a clip from a camera feed.

- Thinking: the model reasons step by step before answering. This helps it better understand user inputs and solve harder visual questions such as math, charts, and multi-step problems.

- Spatial and embodied reasoning: the model’s ability to localize objects and reason about their spatial relationships provides a strong foundation for downstream robotics applications.

LFM3-VL-2B is a leap in performance over the LFM2.5-VL series. Across 62 vision benchmarks, LFM3-VL-2B scores significantly ahead of all models of similar size by at least 7.4 points, and despite its size, it matches the performance of Gemma 4 12B, a model more than 6 times larger, surpasses Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and is within 2 points of GPT-5.6 Luna. Today we're announcing Liquid RIPL (Real-time Inference Pipeline) , a low-latency inference engine built to put Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) directly in the path of a live request. It returns complete generated model responses end-to-end in under 50 ms , and it keeps doing so while traffic arrives continuously at peak load.

Most of today's serving infrastructure is built for a different job: general purpose models, large batches, and long running agentic workflows where a few seconds per request is acceptable. Enterprise real-time workloads have far smaller latency budgets. Search rankings, product recommendations, fraud decisions, payment authorizations, and other real-time workloads need an answer in milliseconds. Even small delays add friction to the user experience, like a slower checkout that hurts conversion. That's why these systems have traditionally used fast, but less accurate, methods like gradient-boosted trees or small embedding models.

Liquid’s RIPL changes that trade off. It’s built for real-time constraints, delivering faster, more responsive generative AI experiences that improve how customers search, discover, transact, and interact.

In Figure 1, we highlight a few different use cases for small LLMs in real time enterprise workflows, enabled by low-latency LLM inference.

## Proven in production

Shopify is deploying LFMs in production across latency-sensitive commerce workloads, where fast and reliable inference is critical to delivering seamless user experiences under high request volumes. One example is search enhancement , where LFMs enable sub-20ms inference on real production workloads . LFMs using ~50% fewer parameters outperform alternatives while delivering 2–10× faster inference , without compromising quality. This is exactly where efficient, task-specialized models shine, especially when paired with high-performance inference engines like Liquid's RIPL to deliver extremely low end-to-end latency and high throughput at scale.
